subject: chemistry
question_text: Calculate the normality of an oxalic acid solution containing 6.3 g of H₂C₂O₄·2H₂O in 500 mL of solution.

verification.note: Chapter 5 (Stoichiometry) is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.66-72), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Equivalent weight and formula
lines: Basicity of oxalic acid = 2 (two acidic H)

lines.text: Normality N = (weight / GEW) × (1000 / V in mL)

steps.why: Normality counts gram equivalents per litre. Oxalic acid gives two H⁺ per molecule, so its equivalent weight is half its molar mass — and the molar mass must include the two water molecules of crystallisation.
common_mistakes: Using 90 (anhydrous H₂C₂O₄) instead of 126 for the hydrated acid.
Dividing by basicity 1. Oxalic acid is dibasic: GEW = 126/2 = 63.
steps.memory_tip: Hydrated oxalic acid: 90 for the acid plus 36 for the two waters gives 126, and dibasic halves it to 63.
steps.margin_note: GEW = 63 with the basicity shown earns this mark.

steps.label: The answer with its unit
steps.why: 6.3/63 = 0.1 gram equivalent in 500 mL; one litre is twice 500 mL, so one litre holds 0.2 gram equivalents.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the 1000/500 = 2 factor and answering 0.1 N.
Writing the answer without the unit N.
steps.memory_tip: Half a litre holds 0.1 equivalent, so the full litre holds 0.2.
steps.margin_note: Box 0.2 N. The unit N (gram equivalents per litre) is part of the mark.

insider_note: Two traps in one two-marker: the water of crystallisation inside 126, and the basicity 2 inside 63. The examiner reads the GEW line before anything else.
